1.pericope_label: The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. And he said, The Lord will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the roar as a prolonged thunder-peal reverberating from the metropolis to the northern promontory, so that the whole country is summoned; Keil and Delitzsch settle the prophet's station against the wealthy reading, the word signifying a rearer of sheep rather than an owner, and state the rule that the numbers three and four denote only multiplicity.

Gill says nothing was spoken of the prophet's own; Calvin explains the verb as meaning to see by revelation and grants the incongruity of speaking of seeing words, argues from the smallness of the town that the shepherd was poor, turns that into a rebuke of the king's pride, and hears in the roar an implied opposition between the one mountain and the rival sanctuaries.

Clarke doubts the prophet was a native of the Judean town, puts him among the very lowest orders of life, and regrets that the translators did not keep the second verse in its four-line form; Wesley notes that all was received by revelation and gives the roar a polemical edge, Jerusalem being the seat of worship and kingdom from which the ten tribes had revolted.

Henry answers his own question whether words can be seen, since the apostles speak of a word of life they had looked upon and handled, lays out both cases for a rich or a poor shepherd, and draws the rule that men are not to be despised for the meanness of their beginnings.

debates.question: Was the prophet a rich flock-owner or a poor shepherd?

positions.position: A simple shepherd: the word signifies a rearer of sheep, not merely an owner, and he says so himself elsewhere.
Poor: the word can mean a wealthy owner, but the town was small and of no opulence, and calling himself a shepherd pours contempt on the king's pride.
Among the very lowest orders of life, tending others' flocks and gathering wild fruit for subsistence.
Either: some think a rich dealer in cattle, others a poor keeper who also gathered wild figs.
A native of the Judean town, living with the shepherds who fed in the neighbouring steppe.
There is no good proof he was a native; he probably retired there when driven out, and was born within the northern territories his mission addressed.

outliers.claim: Reads the roar from Zion as directed against rival worship rather than against enemies, so that those who imagined they honoured the God of their fathers with greater displays than at Jerusalem were in fact worshipping their own devices.

themes: The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
And he said, The Lord will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither.

3.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron: But I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Ben–hadad. I will break also the bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitant from the plain of Aven, and him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden: and the people of Syria shall go into captivity unto Kir, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the numerical formula recurs eight times in these oracles and is idiomatic for repeated delinquencies, corrects the following clause to say God will not turn back the judgment purposed, and would emend the first place-name on the authority of the old Greek; Keil and Delitzsch state the same rule about the numbers and give the oracle plainly.

Gill gives four reasons why the oracles begin with the neighbours rather than with Israel; Calvin states the same as an objection before answering it, holds that the threatening would have seemed accidental had it fallen on Israel alone, takes the bar as a part standing for all the strongholds, and thinks the two place-names probably proper names to whose meanings the prophet alludes.

Clarke turns the numerical formula into an essay on classical usage, quoting Greek and Latin poets who use three and four for repetition and excess, and identifies the places and the region of exile from ancient authorities; Wesley states the formula briefly and puts the exile in Media.
Henry frames the oracles by another prophet's phrase about evil neighbours, observes that the sin specified in each case is persecution, and alone refuses the merely idiomatic reading of the numbers.

debates.question: What do the three transgressions and four mean?

positions.position: A certain number for an uncertain: multiplicity, with the exact count of no consequence.
Repetition and excess, a form of speech used by the most correct writers of antiquity for a finite number standing for an infinite.
Either many, or three and four making seven, a number of perfection showing the measure filled, or three sins with a fourth especially specified.

debates.question: What are the two place-names in the oracle against Damascus?

positions.position: Names of the valley of Damascus, the first a city at the end of the long valley between the two ranges.
The first should be emended on the authority of the old Greek, the Masoretic vocalisation not being what the prophet wrote; the second cannot be determined.
Probably proper names, but the prophet alludes to their meanings, so that the plains near Damascus would be emptied.

outliers.claim: Documents the numerical formula from classical literature at length, quoting the shipwrecked hero who calls those thrice and four times happy that fell at Troy, the Latin poet's version of the cry, an old gloss that it means a finite number for an infinite, and two further instances.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron:
But I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Ben–hadad.

I will break also the bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitant from the plain of Aven, and him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden: and the people of Syria shall go into captivity unto Kir, saith the Lord.

6.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom: But I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza, which shall devour the palaces thereof: And I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him that holdeth the sceptre from Ashkelon, and I will turn mine hand against Ekron: and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the charge as carrying away captives in full number for delivery to the neighbouring people, and note that one city is named where the Philistines generally are meant.

Gill offers five fulfilments of the threatened fire without choosing among them, and adds an Assyrian capture and a later burning for the neighbouring city; Calvin fills in the political background of a hostile people holding land within the allotment, disposes of an etymology of the city's name as frivolous, distinguishes the older city from the later one built nearer the sea, and reads the list of cities as meaning that no place of flight would be safe.

Clarke names the five lordships and their position on the coast, reads the captivity as the fruit of incursions made in times of peace, and reports the marginal rendering of an entire captivity from which none returned; Wesley agrees on the totality and identifies the buyers as the people's most inveterate enemies.

debates.question: What was the scale and occasion of the captivity?

positions.position: The fruit of inroads and incursions made in times of peace; the margin makes it an entire captivity from which none returned.
All the captives they had taken, delivered to the people's most inveterate enemies.

debates.question: Why is the city so named?

positions.position: Not from a Persian word for treasure, as some say, since the Greeks regularly render the Hebrew consonant so and the name preceded that king; rather from its strength.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes two cities of the same name, the older demolished and a later one built nearer the sea, which is why a later writer can describe the place as desert; the prophet threatens the older, and the destruction predicted here is what moved the city to the shore.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom:
But I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza, which shall devour the palaces thereof:

And I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him that holdeth the sceptre from Ashkelon, and I will turn mine hand against Ekron: and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, saith the Lord God.

9.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Tyrus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they delivered up the whole captivity to Edom, and remembered not the brotherly covenant: But I will send a fire on the wall of Tyrus, which shall devour the palaces thereof.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the covenant as the league between the Phoenician king and two kings of Israel, forgotten in mercantile cupidity; Keil and Delitzsch make the kinship of the next nation the whole point of its oracle, no particular sins being charged but only an implacable mortal hatred towards a brother nation.

Gill names three possible fulfilments of the fire without settling; Calvin hesitates over the royal-friendship reading of the covenant as possibly too strained, prefers that the offence was selling brethren to those known to be brethren, and argues from the city's later republican government that its devastation must have preceded Alexander.

Clarke offers the royal league and then a rival reading by which the covenant means the kinship of the two peoples descended from two brothers, and traces the ruin through the long Babylonian siege to Alexander and the fishermen's nets of his own day; Wesley states the covenant plainly as the league between the three kings.

positions.position: The league made between the Phoenician king and the two kings of Israel in succession.
Either that league, or the kinship between the Jews and the Edomites, descended from two brothers.
Perhaps neither: the royal-friendship reading may be too strained, and the offence is rather selling brethren to buyers who knew them to be brethren.

debates.question: When did the fire fall on the city?

positions.position: Undecided among an Assyrian expedition, the thirteen-year Babylonian siege, and the seven-month siege by Alexander.
The Babylonian siege ended in its destruction and Alexander finally ruined it.
It cannot be known with certainty, but not Alexander: by his time the city had no king but a republic, so its devastation was earlier, by the Assyrians, after which it recovered.

outliers.claim: Draws from the selling of brethren the rule that a man who conspires for the ruin of his own brother is a monstrous thing, and that whoever does not abhor a share in such a crime is implicated in it.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Tyrus, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they delivered up the whole captivity to Edom, and remembered not the brotherly covenant:
But I will send a fire on the wall of Tyrus, which shall devour the palaces thereof.

11.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever: But I will send a fire upon Teman, which shall devour the palaces of Bozrah.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers stifled to cast off and reconstructs the two clauses as an indignation that rended continually and a wrath that lurked ever on the watch, while allowing that another punctuation yields the received sense, and he supplies the literary and geographical associations of the two cities; Keil and Delitzsch note that no particular sins are charged, only an implacable hatred, and render the verb as stifling compassion.

Gill supplies the origin of the nation's name from the red pottage and locates the first city from two ancient authorities; Calvin makes the shared circumcision and common father the aggravation, treats the singular number as deliberate so that two brothers and even twins stand before us, and reports two rival constructions of the disputed phrase as strained and improper.

Clarke keeps to history and thinks the part taken in distressing the Jews at the siege of Jerusalem is what the prophet has in view; Wesley reads the clauses as watching for every occasion to oppress and tearing as a ravenous lion tears its prey.

debates.question: How should the clauses about anger and compassion be rendered?

positions.position: Stifled rather than cast off; his indignation rended continually and his wrath lurked ever on the watch, though another punctuation yields the received sense.
He stifles his sympathy or compassionate love.
The disputed phrase is not to be rendered their own bowels, nor transferred to the sons of Jacob, which is strained and improper.
Most probably the part taken in distressing the Jews when Jerusalem was besieged and taken.
Arming themselves alongside heathen nations against their own kindred, perhaps when the Assyrian came or earlier.
No particular offence: an implacable hatred breaking out at every opportunity.

outliers.claim: Treats the singular number, which he calls an anomaly since a whole people is meant, as deliberate: the prophet sets two men before us who were really brothers and even twins, so that the barbarity of venting rage against one's own blood may be felt.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever:
But I will send a fire upon Teman, which shall devour the palaces of Bozrah.

13.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border: But I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour the palaces thereof, with shouting in the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind: And their king shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the precise atrocity is not recorded but that such modes of warfare are darkly conveyed in other passages and throughout the Assyrian inscriptions, rejects the versions that read the last word as the name of the national god, and draws the conclusion of the whole series, that the prophet condemns every violation of the natural laws of which he regards God as custodian; Keil and Delitzsch guess the occasion may have been the Syrian wars, when the border was widened by conquest.

Gill traces the descent through Lot and gives both readings of the last verse without choosing, noting that conquerors commonly carried away the gods of nations they subdued; Calvin makes Abraham the common father of both nations, refuses an emendation that would read mountains for pregnant women, and decides the last verse by the wording, since the text says their king, he and his princes.

Clarke locates the country and its capital, says the atrocity was well known then though the sacred historians give no distinct mention, and thinks the last word should probably be read as the national god with his priesthood; Wesley states the motive without the horror, the border enlarged by destroying all who might claim title to it.

debates.question: Does the last verse speak of the king or of the national god?

positions.position: Probably the god, the princes then being the body of his priesthood.
The king: the received rendering is supported by the old Greek, the Targum and the context, against the Syriac and Vulgate.
The king, since the text says their king, he and his princes, joining him with his nobles.
Either, without choosing between them.

debates.question: Should the word rendered pregnant women be emended?

positions.position: No: some read mountains, driven to it by finding the atrocity strange, and others take mountains metaphorically for fortified cities, which is too strained; the word bears its usual sense.

outliers.claim: Draws the conclusion of the whole series of oracles, that the prophet has been denouncing the sin which trifles with blood, covenants and ancient agreements and recognising the responsibilities of race, but on closer inspection condemns every violation of those natural laws and rights of which he regards God as custodian and executor.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border:
But I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour the palaces thereof, with shouting in the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind:
And their king shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, saith the Lord.
